newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian slide survivor speaks, rescue said near.
newsitem.headline: Australian slide survivor speaks, rescue said near.

text.p: Rescuers were attempting to reach a man found alive on Saturday under the rubble of two Australian ski lodges destroyed in a landslide more than two days ago.
"A miracle has occurred...," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters. "They have made voice contact with a male person and he is certainly alive."
He added: "Ambulance officers are in the cavity, some metres from reaching him. He is conscious and alert and talking to paramedics, which are two to three metres away from him."

The landslide entombed 20 people near midnight on Wednesday at Thredo, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney, and Australia's most popular skiing resort. Three deaths have been confirmed but only one body has been recovered.
Rescuers had all but given up hope of finding a survivor from the twisted wreckage of the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges and the fear of more landslides frequently suspended the rescue operation.
But just after dawn on Saturday rescuers heard muffled sounds and detected muscle movement under a concrete slab.
Frantic rescuers dug by hand to try to reach the trapped man. "It does appear there is sufficient room around him to allow movement," said Sanderson.
Rescuer workers were trying to get oxygen to the man, who has told them he has little feeling in his body. He has not been identified.
Police said they hoped to pull the man from the wreckage soon but there were concerns that shifting wreckage could crush him if rescue crews moved too quickly.
"If what we do under there for example forces the slab to drop our efforts will be vain," Sanderson said.
"The slab is secured to the best of our ability but we're unable to lift it. It would be extremely periolous to make any effort to remove it."
Rescuers said there was a sense of euphoria around the landslide site, where about 100 rescuers were working.
Search crews have been working in the wreckage in freezing conditions for two nights and days, increasingly despairing of finding anyone alive.
Police on Friday had virtually ruled out the chance of finding a survivor, saying the likelihood was "infinitesimally small."

Massive slabs of concrete, where people are believed to be buried, were being painstakingly sawn into pieces before being hoisted free. Conditions were so cold that the water being used to cool the saws was freezing.
Frustration had earlier begun to show on the faces of search crews whose efforts were being stalled by the instability of the slope and fears that the mass of debris could slide further.
Family and friends of the victims have kept a grim vigil on the search, watching from a facing hillside.
